newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Swedish Social Democrats return to lead in polls.
newsitem.headline: Swedish Social Democrats return to lead in polls.

text.p: Sweden's ruling Social Democrats clawed back some popular support in June, regaining the lead from the conservative opposition for the first time in five months, according to a poll released on Sunday.

The survey by the Swedish Institute for Public Opinion Research (SIFO) showed support for the minority Social Democrats rose to 33.7 percent in June from 31.3 percent in May, putting the party back at the top.
Support for the Moderates, as the conservative opposition is known, slipped to 31.7 percent from 33.7 percent.
Sweden's next general election is set for September 1998.

The newspaper Svenska Dagbladet, which published the poll, said the government's upbeat spring budget with optimistic forecasts, released in April, had boosted support for Prime Minister Goran Persson's Social Democrats.
The ruling party suffered in the polls earlier this year with support falling to 27.6 percent in March, the party's lowest rating since April 1991.

Political analysts blamed the slump on continuing high unemployment and the goverment's decision to start phasing out Sweden's nuclear energy next year. This has angered the business community and trade unions.
Svenska Dagbladet said the poll showed that Moderate leader Carl Bildt's return to Swedish politics this month after more than two years in Bosnia had not moved voters.

Bildt, who was prime minister in 1991-94, returned to Sweden this week after ending his position as the major powers' High Representative in Bosnia. He came back to the domestic political arena to prepare his party for the next election.

Among the other five parties in Sweden's parliament, support for the Left Party slipped to 10.5 percent in the June poll from 11.5 percent in May, the Centre Party won 5.9 percent of support against 5.4 percent last month, and the Liberals rose to 6.0 percent from 5.4 percent.
Support for the Christian Democrats dipped to 3.7 percent from 4.1 percent and for the Greens to 7.2 percent from 7.5 percent. Remaining interviewees -- 1.3 percent -- were undecided.
SIFO interviewed 3,516 people between May 26 and June 18 for the latest poll.
